title: Breadboard Anatomy Explorer
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Electronics
description: An interactive half-size (400 tie point) solderless breadboard. Clicking a power rail, a five-hole terminal-strip row, a column, a single tie point, or the center gutter highlights every tie point in that group and explains what it is. A toggle reveals the hidden internal wiring, including the deliberate break at the gutter.

educational.topic: Breadboard internal connections, tie points, power rails, and grid numbering
learningObjectives: Identify the power rails, terminal-strip rows, columns, tie points, and gutter of a half-size solderless breadboard
State the grid address of any hole as a row letter plus a column number
Explain which holes on a breadboard are electrically connected to each other and which are not
Explain why the gutter splits a column into two unconnected groups of five tie points
Explain why the top and bottom power rails require a jumper wire to be connected
prerequisites: A circuit needs a complete path
Two points joined by metal are electrically the same point

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Click-to-reveal labeling with a toggleable overlay, matched to a Remember/Understand objective. The learner explores the board region by region at their own pace rather than watching an animation.
keyQuestions: Which holes on this board are already connected to each other?
Why does a whole column need two colors when a five-hole row needs only one?
How many tie points does one power rail have, and why is it not one per column?
What is the gutter for, and what happens to a lead plugged into it?
commonMisconceptions: A whole column is one connection - it is not; the gutter splits it into two groups of five
Every column has a power rail hole - rail holes come in groups of five with a gap between groups, giving 25 per rail rather than 30
The top and bottom power rails are connected to each other - they are separate until a jumper connects them
The holes in the center channel are usable tie points - they connect to nothing
assessmentOpportunities: Ask students to state a hole's grid address before clicking it
Ask students to predict a power rail's tie-point count before revealing it
Ask students to explain why a chip must straddle the gutter

limitations: This is the bare board only - no components, no current, and no circuit solver. Electrical behavior is introduced in the Push Button and LED Circuit MicroSim.
The board is modeled with 30 tie columns, matching a 400 tie point half-size board. Full-size (830 tie point) boards and boards with split power rails are not shown.
Regions are selected with the mouse or by tapping; there is no keyboard navigation.
